progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: B4 to B5b and the single-celled organisms video: DNA is a double helix of two strands with four bases (A, T, C, G) copied accurately before division; a chromosome is one long DNA molecule, and the human body cell has 46 in two sets of 23; chromosomes are condensed for mitosis; bacteria divide by binary fission, have no nucleus, pass DNA by conjugation and can be antibiotic resistant; mitochondria release energy from food and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; opposite charges attract. Not assumed: prokaryote, eukaryote, nucleoid, plasmid, histone, nucleosome, chromatin, circular and linear molecules, supercoiling, endosymbiosis.
progression.startsWith: About two metres of DNA in a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across, and the question of how a cell stores DNA this long and still uses it, with a bacterium that has no nucleus for comparison.
progression.stopsAfter: Saying the difference is where DNA is kept and how it is arranged, not what it is made of; naming prokaryote and eukaryote by the nucleus; describing a bacterium's usual DNA (one circular chromosome in the nucleoid, no membrane, coiled and held by proteins) and plasmids; describing a eukaryote's DNA (several linear chromosomes in a nucleus, wound on histones as nucleosomes and chromatin, loosened to read a gene and tightened for division); describing the small circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts and why it looks bacterial; comparing the forms side by side; applying all of it to an unseen drawing and an unseen claim. No Griffith or Avery history, no transformation, no archaeal histones, no nucleosome numbers, no transcription detail.
progression.nextLesson: B6b: how a cell reads one gene by copying a section of DNA into mRNA.

teaching.task: Compare how DNA is arranged in a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell and explain why the arrangement matters.
teaching.causalExplanation: Both cell types store genes in the same double helix, so the difference is where it is kept and how it is arranged. A bacterium has no nucleus, so its main DNA is one ring lying in the membrane-free nucleoid, and because the ring is several hundred times longer than the cell, enzymes twist it and proteins grip the coils to hold it compact, with plasmids as small separate rings. A eukaryote keeps several linear chromosomes in a nucleus, and because DNA is negatively charged and histones positively charged, the thread winds on histones into nucleosomes and chromatin. The winding is adjustable, so the cell can loosen the thread to read a gene and tighten it before division. Mitochondria and chloroplasts keep their own small rings because they came from bacteria.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on two metres of thread in a tennis-ball nucleus, keeps one fixed split board of bacterium and eukaryote cell throughout, dims the half not being explained, explains each cause before naming the term, uses a thread-on-spool picture and a twisted rubber band with their limits stated, builds the side-by-side table, teaches the compare sentence frame, and checks with two short unseen items.
teaching.openingDecision: If you unwound the DNA in one of your cells you would have a thread about two metres long in a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across. How does a cell store it and still use it, and does a bacterium do it differently?
teaching.understandingCheck: For two drawn cells where Q has a nucleus holding 8 chromosomes, say which is the prokaryote with one piece of evidence and where Q has other DNA and its shape; then correct the claim that bacterial DNA floats loose and that 46 is all of a human cell's DNA.
teaching.curriculumScope: Construct appropriate representations to model and compare the forms in which DNA exists in eukaryotes and prokaryotes (Module 5, p1045). The learner construction stays with the practical-style video. Griffith and Avery, transformation, archaeal histones, nucleosome numbers and transcription are held back.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, one deep plum DNA thread colour for every ring, rod and thread, warm sand histone spools, dashed ink rings for membranes and solid ink for walls, a fixed split board (bacterium left, eukaryotic cell right), thread and spool winding, a coiling ring, scale bars and a compare table. Amber is the tag and emphasis colour; blue and green are not used.
design.transitionPlan: The hook board splits into the fixed bacterium and eukaryote halves; the half not being explained dims to about 30 per cent through scenes 3 to 9; camera pushes reach the bacterium and the rod; the spool plate fades while the wound discs stay; the compare table builds on the same split board with both halves at full strength and stays for the sentence frame; the attempt boards remove the aids and the feedback rebuilds the drawing and the claim card; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
